Ah, the glorious freedom of the blank page—or the blank screen, in this case. Where to begin? Maybe with the way light slants through a window at 3:47 PM, painting everything in gold and shadow, like a Rembrandt who forgot to finish the painting. Or perhaps with the absurdity of how we humans spend entire lives chasing things that don’t even exist—like "happiness" or "success"—while the real magic is in the tiny, unnoticed moments: the first sip of coffee in the morning, the way a stranger’s laugh sounds like a secret you weren’t meant to hear, or the quiet thrill of realizing you’ve finally memorized the lyrics to a song you’ve hated for years.

Speaking of songs, what if music was just a way for the universe to communicate with itself? Like, imagine if every note was a tiny cosmic handshake between galaxies, and we’re just the lucky few who get to eavesdrop. That would explain why some songs make you cry and others make you want to dance like a maniac in a parking lot. (I’ve done both. Multiple times.)

And then there’s the internet—a vast, chaotic library of cat videos, conspiracy theories, and people arguing about whether pineapple belongs on pizza (it does, fight me). It’s both the greatest invention and the most terrifying experiment in human history. One minute you’re learning how to fold a fitted sheet, the next you’re down a rabbit hole about 19th-century tax laws in Mongolia. The internet is like a fire: warm and useful, but also capable of burning down the house if you’re not careful.

What about time? We’re all just temporary tenants in this weird, spinning rock hurtling through space, and yet we act like we own the place. We stress over deadlines, birthdays, and the fact that we’ll one day turn into dust, but we never stop to marvel at how bizarre it is that we’re *here at all*. A few billion years ago, there was nothing. Now there’s *you*, reading this, and me, typing it, and somewhere out there, a squirrel judging our life choices. The universe is under no obligation to make sense, and yet here we are, making up stories to explain it all.

And what about love? Not the grand, Hollywood kind, but the small, stubborn love—the way your dog tilts its head when you’re sad, or how your best friend knows exactly what you need before you do. Love isn’t just a feeling; it’s a verb. It’s showing up, even when it’s hard. It’s choosing someone (or something) every single day, even when you’d rather not.

I could go on forever—about the way books smell like old paper and adventure, or how a single raindrop can feel like a blessing, or why we’re all so obsessed with finding "the one" when maybe the real treasure is the people who stick around when you’re messy, broken, and still figuring it out.

But perhaps the most beautiful thing is that none of this has to make sense. We don’t need answers. We just need to keep showing up, curious and a little bit afraid, and trust that the universe—messy, wonderful, absurd universe—has our backs.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I need to go stare out the window and wonder what the clouds are thinking. (Spoiler: They’re probably judging us too.)
